title: Introduction and Rondo capriccioso in A minor
hook: Nine minutes for a young Spanish violinist, a sad song and then a dance that never quite lands where you expect.

painting.title: Lorenzo Pagans and Auguste De Gas
painting.pairingNote: A Spanish musician playing in a Paris drawing room, with Degas’s father listening, head bowed; the same Paris that fell for Spanish music in the 1860s, when Saint-Saëns wrote this piece for the young Spanish violinist Pablo de Sarasate.

facts: Saint-Saëns wrote this piece in 1863 for Pablo de Sarasate, a Spanish violinist nine years younger who had come to study in Paris as a boy. Saint-Saëns had already written a concerto for him in 1859, when Sarasate was only 15; the Introduction and Rondo capriccioso came next. Sarasate gave the first performance in Paris on 4 April 1867, with the composer conducting.

It is a showpiece in two parts played without a break: a short, sad song, then a fast [[rondo|rondo]], a form in which one tune keeps coming back between new episodes. *Capriccioso* means whimsical: the rondo tune hesitates, skips and lands on the wrong beats.

Paris in those years loved anything Spanish, and the rondo has the lilt of a Spanish dance, with sharp off-beat accents and sudden swerves. It made the piece a favourite of violinists from the start. Georges Bizet, the future composer of *Carmen*, arranged it for violin and piano, and his version was printed in 1869, ten years before the orchestral score.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a melancholy song with a flash of fireworks, then a skittish dance that returns again and again, and a race to the finish.

movements.heading: Andante malinconico – Allegro ma non troppo
movements.tempo: Andante malinconico – Allegro ma non troppo
movements.summary: The introduction is a sad, sighing song for the violin over quiet chords, broken once by a sudden burst of fast notes. Then the rondo begins: a jumpy, syncopated tune that comes back several times, with more lyrical tunes and dazzling passages in between. Near the end the music speeds up and the violin races to the last chords.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a melancholy melody, slow and close to speech, marked *Andante malinconico* (“walking, melancholy”).

mainIdeas.name: The rondo tune
mainIdeas.description: short, light phrases that start off the beat, as if the violin were hesitating before each step. Its [[syncopation|syncopation]] gives it a Spanish swagger.

mainIdeas.name: The episodes
mainIdeas.description: a smoother, singing melody, and passages of rapid runs and leaps that test the soloist.

stops.hear: Soft chords in the orchestra; the violin sings a slow, sad melody, with little sighs
Suddenly the violin breaks into a rush of very fast notes, then settles back into the song
stops.happening: The *Animato*: a first flash of virtuosity

stops.hear: Faster: the violin plays a jumpy tune in short, off-beat phrases over light chords
stops.happening: The Rondo begins. This is the tune that keeps returning

stops.hear: The full orchestra bursts in loudly with the tune
The violin turns to a smoother, more singing melody
The jumpy tune is back in the violin
stops.happening: The first return of the rondo theme

stops.hear: A broader, warmer melody, then rapid passages and leaps across the strings
Faster and faster: the violin rushes up and down the instrument, brighter now

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A last dash and a few short, loud chords

notice: Tap your foot to the rondo tune. Its accents fall where you do not expect them, and the violin seems to arrive a moment late or early. That is the *capriccioso*.
Compare the end with the beginning: a piece that opens in sorrow ends in a blaze.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Perlman made this album with Jean Martinon and the Orchestre de Paris in July 1974, together with Saint-Saëns’s *Havanaise*, Chausson’s *Poème* and Ravel’s *Tzigane*. Martinon had himself trained as a violinist at the Paris Conservatoire.

threads.title: Written for a player
threads.body: Saint-Saëns wrote his First and Third Violin Concertos, and this piece, for Sarasate. Sarasate’s light, pure tone and easy speed are built into the music: few long, heavy notes, many quick, clean ones.

threads.title: Spanish Paris
threads.body: Bizet’s *Carmen*, Lalo’s *Symphonie espagnole*, also for Sarasate, and this rondo all come from the same French fascination with Spain.

threads.title: Sorrow, then sparkle
threads.body: The slow, sad introduction is short, but it makes the rondo’s high spirits sound brighter.
